specification: Wire format v1, revision 3. Eleven '\n'-separated fields: domain, audience, key id, method, canonical path, query, body SHA-256, Content-Type, organization, timestamp, nonce. Field 9 ({organization}) is the Perceivo-Organization header verbatim, the empty string when absent. The nonce is last.
secret_note: This key is PUBLISHED ON PURPOSE and protects nothing. A vector table is a (audience, key_id, method, path, query, body, content_type, organization, timestamp, nonce, secret) -> signature mapping, so the key has to be in the file or no independent implementation can reproduce a single row. It is a fixed test constant, identical in every copy of this file, and already known to anyone who can read the SDK. Never configure it as a signing key for any environment: a request signed with it is signed by everyone. Static scanners flag its presence here (CodeQL py/clear-text-storage-sensitive-data); that finding is correct about the shape and wrong about the risk.

secret_transport.note: HOW A SECRET SPELLING BECOMES AN HMAC KEY. The HMAC key is 32 raw bytes. What this platform DISCLOSES to a customer, once, at enrolment, is those bytes rendered as 64 lowercase hex characters. So the caller holds text, the verifier holds bytes, and an implementation must DECODE the disclosure — never encode it. UTF-8-encoding the disclosure produces a 64-byte key against the server's 32-byte one and every request fails with an ordinary 401 that names no cause. secret_utf8 above is 31 bytes and is NOT this shape, so no positive vector in this file exercises the disclosure encoding; secret_transport_vectors does, including the signature the wrong encoding produces so the bug is identifiable rather than merely present.
secret_transport.disclosure_secret_note: A SECOND published test constant, distinct from secret_utf8 and protecting nothing. It exists because a table whose every row keys on a 31-byte ASCII string cannot observe the encoding this platform actually uses. Never configure it anywhere.
secret_transport.rule: A str of exactly 64 characters drawn from [0-9a-fA-F] is the disclosure and is hex-decoded; any other str is keyed on its own UTF-8 bytes; a bytes value is the key verbatim. Hex decoding is case-insensitive. Surrounding whitespace is stripped before the shape is tested, because a disclosure read from a file or a shell carries a trailing newline and a newline is not key material.
secret_transport.residual: A genuine 64-character passphrase drawn entirely from the hex alphabet is indistinguishable from a disclosure by inspection and IS decoded. The collision is resolved in favour of the disclosure because this platform issues only the disclosure shape. A caller who means 'key on this text' says so by passing bytes.

notes: ELEVEN fields, TEN '\n' separators, NO trailing newline. Field 1 is the constant 'perceivo-hmac-v1' and is never configurable; field 2 is the audience; field 3 is the key id; field 8 is Content-Type; field 9 is the organization. The nonce is LAST and that is load-bearing: no field follows it for an injected newline to forge a boundary into. An implementation that moves any field to the end signs a different string.

Fields 1-3 and 9 must be BOUND, not merely present. A field that is in the string but is never compared against a value the verifier holds itself buys nothing: the attacker sets it to whatever makes the mac verify. Field 1 is compared for exact equality; field 2 to the verifier's own configured audience; field 3 to the id of the key whose secret was fetched. Field 8 is deliberately NOT bound at the origin — it is signed so it cannot be altered in flight, and the framework re-reads the header for parsing anyway.

⛔ FIELD 8's NO-BINDING ARGUMENT DOES NOT GENERALISE TO FIELD 9. Field 8 needs no binding because there is nothing at the verifier to compare it against. Field 9 SELECTS THE TENANT the authorization decision runs against, so the value that entered field 9 and the value the tenancy decision uses must be PROVED to be the same value. A field 9 that is signed but never re-derived at the verifier buys NOTHING and reads as present, which is worse than absent. Bind it AFTER compare_digest, never before: both sides of that comparison are client-asserted, so run early it compares attacker input against attacker input and proves nothing at all. Vector n07 is what distinguishes an implementation that binds it from one that merely signs it.

The negative_vectors list carries CORRECTLY SIGNED canonical strings that must be REFUSED. Against a bare mac check every one of them passes. All must be refused with ONE indistinguishable outcome — a distinct reason per check is an oracle.

⛔ THE NEGATIVE CLASS SPLITS IN THREE, and conflating the parts produces a GREEN SUITE OVER A BROKEN CHANGE. Each row declares 'refused_by': 'arity' rows (n01, n02, n06) are refused on the field COUNT before anything else runs; 'prelude_binding' rows (n03, n04, n05) carry the FULL ELEVEN FIELDS and are refused on the CONTENT of fields 1-3; the 'metadata_binding' row (n07) carries eleven correct prelude fields and is refused only AFTER the mac, on field 9. Leaving n03/n04/n05 at ten fields would keep them green while silently substituting their failure cause with arity — the domain-separator, audience and key-id checks would then be entirely untested, and the hazard's only signature is a PASSING TEST. Assert 'field_count' per row, not merely that the row was refused.

The audience is a DEPLOYMENT LABEL, server-assigned and configured on both sides. It is NOT a hostname, NOT the Host header and NOT derived from the request in any way; a verifier that reads it from the request compares the attacker's value with the attacker's value. Per-key audience scoping is a known follow-on, not an oversight.

key_id is the api_keys.id UUID in lowercase hyphenated 8-4-4-4-12 form — NOT the key prefix, which every key in an organization shares. v28 supplies the SAME uuid in uppercase and must produce v01's signature byte for byte. Normalise by parsing the uuid and re-rendering it, so the only two outcomes are the right signature or a rejection; an implementation that formats whatever string it was handed can emit a silently different one.

content_type is the Content-Type request header VERBATIM: not normalised, not case-folded, parameters NOT stripped. An ABSENT header is the empty string (v01, v29), the same convention the query field uses. v30/v31 are byte-identical bodies whose declared multipart boundary differs and whose signatures therefore differ — a 'canonical media type' that dropped parameters would collapse them to one signature and leave the re-framing attack open. v02, v32 and v33 are three signatures over one set of body bytes.

Sign AFTER the body and headers are final. HTTP client libraries generate the multipart boundary themselves, so a signer invoked before the client sets Content-Type commits to a value the request never carries — and every signed upload then 401s with nothing to see on either side.

No field may contain '\n'. An implementation must not ESCAPE a newline — it must REJECT the request as unsignable. Likewise a Content-Type header that appears more than once is rejected rather than joined or arbitrarily picked from.

Field 8 admits ASCII PRINTABLE 0x20-0x7E ONLY. A Content-Type carrying any other byte is UNSIGNABLE and must be refused at signing time — never escaped, never transliterated, never signed and left for the edge to reject. This is narrower than RFC 7231, which admits obs-text in a quoted-string, and the narrowing is the whole mechanism: on ASCII printable a latin-1 decode and a UTF-8 decode are the identity function, so once neither side can admit anything else the two provably agree without either conceding a charset to the other. The empty value stays legal (v01, v29) — the rule is '*', not '+'.

The unsignable_vectors list is a THIRD kind of vector, distinct from negative_vectors. A negative vector is a CORRECTLY SIGNED string a bound verifier must refuse (mac_is_correct is true for all of them). An unsignable vector has no canonical_request and no signature at all, because the only conforming answer to the input is a refusal to build one. A consumer checks these by attempting to canonicalise and requiring an error.
body_base64 null means NO body; an empty string means a zero-byte body. Both produce the same digest (see v01 and v18).

The HMAC key is the secret's RAW BYTES — never a hex or base64 re-encoding of them. For secret_utf8 those bytes are secret_utf8 encoded UTF-8, which is why every positive vector here keys on secret_utf8 directly. ⛔ DO NOT GENERALISE THAT TO A REAL KEY. A real secret is disclosed as 64 hex characters encoding 32 bytes, and signing with those characters is wrong. The statement is about the KEY and says nothing about the TRANSPORT; secret_transport says what the transport is, and secret_transport_vectors pins it in both directions.

The canonical request is UTF-8 encoded before HMAC. Every POSITIVE vector here is ASCII, because raw_path and the query string are always percent-encoded on the wire and field 8 is now restricted to ASCII printable. That is a property of the table, not a coincidence — and it is also why positive vectors alone cannot observe a field-8 charset divergence; unsignable_vectors covers that.

There is no 'host' field. The signature covers no authority: not the Host header and not an absolute-form request target. The audience serves the purpose a host field would, without letting the attacker choose it.

canonical_path is field 5 and it is the BASE-NORMALISED path, NOT raw_path verbatim. Two operations, in this order: (1) percent-decode UNRESERVED characters only (A-Z a-z 0-9 - . _ ~), both hex cases; (2) remove dot segments per RFC 3986 5.2.4. Nothing else — '//' is not merged, a trailing '/' is not stripped, a reserved escape such as '%2F' is not decoded, and an escape step 1 did not decode is not case-normalised. The platform's ingress applies exactly this transform (pathNormalization: BASE) to every path and NOTHING to the query, and the signature base must be produced by the same transform as the routing key. A signer that emits raw_path verbatim fails v22, v23, v25, v26 and v27; one that reverses the two steps fails v27 alone.

The path transform is deliberately NOT injective. v22, v23 and v24 are three request targets with ONE signature, and so are v25, v26 and v27. A signature commits to an EQUIVALENCE CLASS of targets, not to a target. That is safe only because every member of a class arrives at the origin as the same normalised path, so the class the signature commits to and the class the router cannot distinguish are the same class.

canonical_query is field 6 and is the query string VERBATIM — every byte after the first '?', in the order sent. Nothing is split, sorted, decoded, re-encoded, deduplicated or reassembled. An implementation that sorts fails v03, v04, v06, v15, v20 and v21, and collapses two distinct pairs to a single signature: v19/v20 and v04/v21.

v35 and v36 are the ORGANIZATION PAIR: the same request differing ONLY in the Perceivo-Organization value, published with two DIFFERENT signatures. This is the row that proves the organization is signed. Exactly THREE positive rows sign a non-empty organization — v34, v35 and v36; the other 33 sign the empty string. So if field 9 were dropped in a later refactor those 33 would still pass, and only v34, v35 and v36 would catch it. Compare either against v01, which is the same request with no header at all: three targets, three signatures.

The five unsignable rows u01-u05 carry 'field_number': 8. They have neither a canonical_request nor a signature, and they name the right field because field 9 follows content_type, which holds wire position 8.

u06-u11 are the field 9 unsignable rows ('field_number': 9). Field 9 is REJECTED, never normalised: uppercase, braced and unhyphenated UUIDs are all refused rather than folded to the canonical spelling. ⚠️ This DELIBERATELY DIVERGES from key_id (see v28), which IS normalised. key_id is derived from a uuid the server already resolved, so re-rendering it is total and safe; field 9 is raw client text that must survive byte-identically through a signer, a verifier AND a tenancy decision in three independent implementations. An implementation that reuses its key_id normaliser for field 9 passes v28 and fails u06, u07 and u08.

v19 and v20 are a PERMUTATION PAIR: the same two elements in the two possible orders, published with two DIFFERENT signatures. The origin resolves a repeated key to its LAST occurrence, so the two targets mean opposite things. A verifier that returns the same signature for both is wrong in the direction that matters: it validates a request whose meaning was never signed.

Body-size-cap vectors (a body exactly at the cap, and one byte over, expecting 413) are deliberately NOT in this file. The cap is a server-side admission control, not a canonicalization rule; a multi-megabyte vector would also make this file unusable. The server implementer owns those two cases.

generated_under.note: Vectors are only meaningful relative to a named parser. The values below are what THIS repository can measure; the server parser contract is declared, not measured here.

server_parser_contract.note: Declared by the platform; NOT measured by this repository. If the origin's parser changes, these vectors must be regenerated and re-agreed.

vectors.description: GET with no query and no body. The body field is the SHA-256 of ZERO bytes, never of '{}' and never empty; the query field is the empty string and its separators remain. There is no Content-Type on the request either, so field 8 is the empty string by the same convention.

POST with a compact JSON body. The bytes hashed are the bytes sent — never a re-serialization. Content-Type is 'application/json' with NO parameters; compare v32 and v33, same bytes with parameters, three different signatures.

Query keys arrive in a NON-alphabetical order and are signed in that order. A sorting implementation emits 'archived=false&cursor=abc&limit=10' here and produces a different signature, so this vector fails against one.
A key with no '=' keeps that distinction from a key with an empty value: 'flag' stays 'flag'. Submission order is preserved, so this is 'flag&flag=&a=1', not the sorted 'a=1&flag&flag='.
'?a=' is an empty value, distinct from '?a'.

Repeated keys keep their submission order: 'tag=zeta&tag=alpha&tag=beta' signs in exactly that order. The origin resolves a repeated key to its LAST occurrence, so the order is meaning, not presentation.
%2F in the path is NOT decoded — '/a%2Fb' and '/a/b' are different requests with different signatures.
Percent-encoding case is preserved: '%2f' is not normalized to '%2F'. Compare with v07 — same route, different signature.
'+' in a query value stays '+'. Nothing is decoded and nothing is re-encoded, so '+' is not read as a space.
'//' in the path is preserved, not collapsed.
A non-ASCII path segment is signed in its percent-encoded UTF-8 form (cafe with an acute accent). No Unicode normalization is applied: NFC and NFD spellings are different bytes and sign differently.
A body containing bytes that are not valid UTF-8 (0xff 0xfe 0x00 0x01) hashes fine — the body is hashed as bytes, never as text.
A trailing '/' is significant: compare with v01, same route, different signature.
DELETE with a query and no body — the empty-body digest again.
Empty elements between '&' separators are retained in place, so 'a=1&&b=2' canonicalizes to 'a=1&&b=2'. A sorting implementation moves the empty element to the front and emits '&a=1&b=2'.
An '=' inside a value needs no rule at all when the bytes are emitted verbatim: 'filter=a=b&z=1' signs as itself. There is no key/value split in which the distinction could be lost.
A UTF-8 body with non-ASCII text, hashed as the encoded bytes.

vectors.description: An explicitly empty body (zero bytes) is identical to no body at all.

PERMUTATION PAIR, member A. Together with v20 this is the vector this table exists to carry: the same two elements in the two possible orders. The origin resolves a repeated key to its LAST occurrence, so v19 means org=victim and v20 means org=attacker. Their signatures MUST differ. A sorting implementation returns 'org=attacker&org=victim' for both and produces ONE signature for two different requests.
PERMUTATION PAIR, member B — v19's elements in reverse submission order. Compare the signatures with v19: they must not be equal.

A deliberately NON-alphabetical query whose sorted form differs from its submission form: 'flag=&flag&a=1' signs as itself, where a sorting implementation emits 'a=1&flag&flag='. This vector cannot pass against one.

BASE step 1 decodes UNRESERVED escapes only: '%7e' becomes '~', so the path field is '/api/v1/files/a~b'. Compare with v23 and v24: all three are ONE signature. The transform is deliberately not injective — a signature commits to an equivalence class of targets, because every member of the class reaches the origin as the same normalised path.

BOTH hex cases decode: '%7E' becomes '~' exactly as '%7e' does. Same signature as v22 and v24. Contrast v07/v08, where '%2F' and '%2f' are RESERVED, are not decoded, and therefore keep their hex-case difference and sign differently.
The third member of the class: the character sent literally. A signer that emits raw_path verbatim gives v24 this signature and gives v22 and v23 two others, so it agrees here and fails there.

BASE step 2 removes dot segments (RFC 3986 5.2.4): '/api/v1/x/../components' signs as '/api/v1/components'. httpx already removes them before the wire and Envoy removes them again, so this is the fixed point of every hop — which is exactly why it is the thing to sign.
'/./' is removed too: '/api/v1/./components' signs as '/api/v1/components'. Same signature as v25 and v27.

THE STEP-ORDER DISCRIMINATOR. '%2E' is unreserved, so step 1 decodes it to '.' and step 2 must then treat it as a dot segment: '/api/v1/x/%2E%2E/components' signs as '/api/v1/components'. An implementation that removes dot segments FIRST finds none to remove and emits '/api/v1/x/../components' instead. This is the ONLY vector that separates the two orders. WARNING: this vector pins the CLIENT transform, which the specification fully determines; it is NOT evidence about what the platform's ingress does with '%2E', and it must not be read as any.

THE KEY-ID NORMALISATION VECTOR. 'key_id_input' is the SAME uuid as every other vector's, supplied in UPPERCASE. Field 3 is the lowercase 8-4-4-4-12 form, so this vector's canonical_request and signature are BYTE-IDENTICAL to v01's. An implementation that formats whatever string it was handed produces a different signature here and agrees everywhere else — which is the failure mode this vector exists to catch. Normalise by parsing the uuid and re-rendering it; never assume the value arrived formatted. Braced, unhyphenated and uppercase forms all normalise to the same field 3.

A POST that carries body bytes and NO Content-Type header. Field 8 is the EMPTY STRING — the same convention the query field uses, not a guessed default and not the field's omission. An implementation that defaults an absent header to 'application/octet-stream' produces a different signature here and agrees everywhere else.

BOUNDARY PAIR, member A. The body bytes are BYTE-IDENTICAL to v31 and only the multipart 'boundary' parameter differs. This is the attack field 8 exists to close: re-framing the same signed bytes so the server's multipart parser reads different parts out of them. Because Content-Type is signed VERBATIM, the two sign differently. An implementation that canonicalises to the media type and drops parameters emits ONE signature for both and leaves the attack open.

vectors.description: A well-formed Perceivo-Organization on a request that also carries a body and a Content-Type, so field 9 is exercised in a realistic shape rather than only in isolation. Field 9 is the header VERBATIM, lowercase hyphenated 8-4-4-4-12. Compare with v02, the same request with no organization header: the signatures differ, which is the whole of what field 9 buys.

ORGANIZATION PAIR, member A. Identical to v36 in method, target, body and Content-Type; ONLY the organization differs. THIS IS THE PAIR THAT PROVES THE ORGANIZATION IS SIGNED: exactly THREE positive rows sign a non-empty organization — v34, v35 and v36 — so if field 9 were dropped in a later refactor the other 33 would still pass and only those three would catch it. It is also the same request as v01, which sends no header at all — three targets, three signatures.

ORGANIZATION PAIR, member B — same request, different tenant. Compare the signatures with v35: they must not be equal. An implementation that omits field 9, or that signs a constant there, emits ONE signature for both and leaves cross-tenant replay open: a captured signature for member A is re-presented with member B's header and verifies, and the audit trail then records the action against the VICTIM tenant.

negative_vectors.description: THE SIX-FIELD DOWNGRADE. A six-field string for the SAME request, correctly signed. A verifier that accepts it leaves every other field present in its own canonicaliser and bound to nothing. Refuse on the field count BEFORE comparing digests: eleven fields, ten separators, no trailing newline.
A NINE-field string -- the eleven fields without Content-Type and organization, which a partially updated implementation emits. Same rule: the field count is checked, not tolerated.

Field 1 is 'perceivo-hmac-v2'. ⛔ ELEVEN FIELDS -- the arity is CORRECT here, deliberately, so that the only thing refusing this string is the domain comparison itself. The domain separator is a CONSTANT and is never configurable; it must be compared for exact equality so a signature minted for some future scheme with the same secret cannot be replayed into this one.

Field 2 is 'perceivo-api-prod' where this verifier is configured for 'perceivo-api-local'. ⛔ ELEVEN FIELDS, so the arity check cannot be what refuses it. Correctly signed, and refused: this is the cross-origin replay the audience exists to stop. The verifier compares field 2 to ITS OWN configured audience -- never to the request's Host header, which the attacker chooses.

Field 3 is '3d1c1a7e-6b54-4b0e-9a2d-8c5f0e21b4aa' while the bearer header names '0f8fad5b-d9cb-469f-a165-70867728950e', whose secret was used. ⛔ ELEVEN FIELDS, so the arity check cannot be what refuses it. Correctly signed, and refused: the verifier compares field 3 to the id of the key it actually resolved the secret from, so a signature cannot be presented under a different identity.

⛔ THE ONE AN ATTACKER TRIES FIRST. A TEN-field string -- the eleven fields with field 9 OMITTED rather than empty. It is also exactly what a signer lacking field 9 emits on EVERY request, so this row is the difference between a bare 401 naming no cause and an arity denial a customer can diagnose against the published table. Accepting it means field 9 is unbound and a captured signature is re-aimable at another tenant. ⭐ Note what it is NOT: it is not v01's string, because v01 signs field 9 as the EMPTY string and this one omits the field. Empty and absent are the same VALUE and different ARITIES, and only the arity check can tell them apart.

⛔ THE ROW THAT PROVES FIELD 9 IS BOUND RATHER THAN MERELY SIGNED, and the only row in this list that survives every check before the mac. Eleven fields; fields 1, 2 and 3 are all correct; the mac is correct. Field 9 names '1a4f6d20-9e3b-47c8-85af-b62d0c17e995' while the edge presented '8c7e2b41-5d93-4a06-bf12-3e9d70a5c684' -- see presented_organization. A verifier must re-derive field 9 from the SIGNED string AFTER compare_digest and refuse the disagreement (signature_metadata_unbound), exactly as it already does for the timestamp and the nonce. ⛔ It must NOT do this in the prelude: before the mac, BOTH sides of that comparison are client-asserted, so the check would compare attacker input against attacker input and prove nothing at all. An implementation that signs field 9 and never re-derives it passes every other row in this file and fails only this one -- which is why it exists.

unsignable_vectors.description: THE PARITY VECTOR. A Content-Type whose parameter carries U+00E9, sent as UTF-8 bytes. Field 8 admits ASCII printable 0x20-0x7E only, so the signer must REFUSE rather than sign it. Without the rule the two sides diverge silently: a verifier that decodes the raw header bytes as latin-1 and a signer that decodes them as UTF-8 build DIFFERENT field 8 values for these bytes ('Ã©' vs 'é') and therefore different signatures, and no pure-ASCII positive vector can observe it. On ASCII printable the two decodes are the identity function, so refusing everything else is what makes the encoding question moot rather than answered.

A single 0xFF byte, which is not valid UTF-8 at all. It is refused by the UTF-8 decode before the charset check is reached; the OUTCOME is what the vector pins, not which check produced it. A latin-1 decoder reaches the charset check instead and must refuse there. Either way the request is unsignable and no signature exists for it.

A newline in Content-Type. 0x0A is outside 0x20-0x7E, so the charset rule SUBSUMES the older 'no newline in a field' rule rather than sitting beside it. Still REJECTED, never escaped: escaping would keep the field count right and produce a string no other implementation would reproduce.

A horizontal tab (0x09) between parameters. RFC 7230 admits it as optional whitespace inside a header value, and this format does NOT — the narrowing is deliberate, and it is the kind of case where a permissive implementation and a strict one drift apart silently.
0x7F (DEL) — one past the top of the admitted range. The boundary is closed at 0x7E, so this pins the upper edge; 0x7E itself ('~') is signable and appears in the positive controls.

THE NORMALISATION VECTOR, INVERTED. The same uuid as v35's, spelled in UPPERCASE. field 9 is REJECTED rather than folded to lowercase — which is the exact opposite of v28, where an uppercase key_id normalises to the canonical spelling and produces v01's signature. The divergence is deliberate: key_id is derived from a uuid the SERVER already resolved, so re-rendering it is total and safe, while field 9 is raw client text that must survive byte-identically through a signer, a verifier and a tenancy decision in three independent implementations.
The Microsoft registry-format spelling, in braces. Refused for u06's reason: there is one admissible spelling of field 9 and it is not this one.

The 32-character unhyphenated form. Refused for u06's reason. This is the spelling `uuid.UUID()` accepts most silently, so an implementation that validates by PARSING rather than by MATCHING the grammar accepts it and signs a field the verifier will never reproduce.

A plausible-looking organization SLUG rather than a uuid. Field 9 is the uuid shape or the empty string; nothing else is admissible, and a signer must refuse rather than pass the value through and let it fail as an unexplainable 401.

A newline inside the organization value. REJECTED, never escaped: the field-count check is what catches a smuggled separator, and an injected one must yield TWELVE fields and a denial rather than a forged field boundary. Escaping would keep the arity right and produce a string no other implementation would reproduce.

TWO Perceivo-Organization headers. Rejected rather than resolved, and for a sharper reason than the duplicate Content-Type case: picking one of two values means the VERIFIER and the TENANCY DECISION can pick differently, which is precisely the confusion field 9 exists to close. ⛔ Read the header from the raw header LIST — a mapping built from it collapses duplicates, and the guard then reports green on the one input it exists to refuse.

secret_transport_vectors.description: THE PRODUCTION PATH. The 64-hex disclosure DECODED to its 32 bytes, which are the bytes the server sealed and the bytes it keys on. If your implementation reproduces exactly one row in this list, it must be this one.

⛔ THE DEFECT, PUBLISHED SO IT IS IDENTIFIABLE. The same disclosure UTF-8-ENCODED instead of decoded: a 64-byte key where the server holds a 32-byte one. MUST NOT VERIFY. If your signature for t01 equals THIS value, you have the encode/decode inversion and nothing else — do not go looking at the canonicaliser, the timestamp or the nonce. Every positive row above passes with this bug, because no row above keys on a hex secret.

The same 32 bytes, disclosure spelled in UPPERCASE hex. Hex decoding is case-insensitive and both spellings are the same key, so this signature is IDENTICAL to t01's — asserted at generation time, not hoped for. An implementation that rejects the uppercase spelling, or that lowercases the decoded BYTES rather than the text, fails here.

THE POSITIVE CONTROL ON ADDITIVITY. `secret_utf8` is 31 bytes and is not the hex shape, so it keys on its own UTF-8 bytes: this signature is IDENTICAL to the primary vector's, asserted at generation time. It proves the hex path is a separate branch that leaves non-hex secrets, and every positive vector in the table, unaffected.

64 characters, ONE of them outside the hex alphabet. Keyed on its UTF-8 bytes, because the gate is the alphabet AND the length, not the length alone. A verifier that decodes on length would raise on this input instead of signing it. ⚠️ Note the unresolvable residual this row bounds: a genuine 64-character passphrase drawn ENTIRELY from the hex alphabet is indistinguishable from a disclosure and is decoded. Callers who mean 'key on this text' pass bytes.
